title: One stencil, slid everywhere
allegory: A convolution is like sliding one small stencil across a photo and scoring, at every spot, how well the patch underneath matches it; because the same stencil is reused everywhere, it needs few weights and only ever looks at neighbours.
map: the kernel: a small grid of learned weights, shape (in_channels, k, k)
scoring one spot: multiply the overlapping pairs and add
a dot product of the kernel with one patch of the input
the same stencil carried to every spot
weight sharing: one kernel applied at every position
a ring of blank paper, and how far each hop goes
padding and stride, which set the output size
a second stencil makes a second score sheet
each out_channel is its own kernel with its own feature map
where_else: Every vision network since AlexNet, ResNet included
Max pooling: the same sliding window and size formula, with no learned weights
Transposed convolutions in a GAN generator, doubling the size instead of halving it
The edge and curve detectors interpretability finds in early vision layers

hamming.what: Sliding one small learned grid of weights across an input and taking a dot product at every position.
hamming.when: Whenever the input has spatial structure, where nearby values belong together, as in photographs.
hamming.why: Reusing one kernel everywhere means far fewer weights and a built-in assumption of locality, which is how AlexNet beat a decade of hand-built features.

object.title: The stencil press
object.subtitle: A sheet of score tiles: each one is a spot the stencil visited, raised by how hard it fired.

knobs.label: Stencil: side edges (0) or top edges (1)

cap.1: The photo is dark with a bright square in one corner. Each tile is a spot the stencil visited; tall tiles mean it fired hard.
cap.2: An 8x8 input, a 3x3 side-edge kernel, no padding, stride 1: a 6x6 feature map. The tall tiles trace the square's left side.
cap.3: out[i,j] = Σ_a Σ_b x[i+a, j+b]·w[a,b] with w = [-1, 0, 1] in each row, so L_out = 8 - 3 + 1 = 6. Height is |out|/3.

cap.1: Swap in a different stencil, one that looks for top edges. Same photo, but now the square's top side lights up instead.
cap.2: A second out_channel is a second kernel with its own weights, producing its own feature map from the same input.
cap.3: Each output channel owns a kernel of shape (in_channels, k, k); stacking them gives the weight tensor (out, in, k, k).

cap.1: Back to the side-edge stencil, now with a ring of blank paper round the photo. The sheet grows back to 8 by 8.
cap.2: padding=1 with a 3x3 kernel at stride 1 keeps the size: 8 + 2 - 3 + 1 = 8. That is what makes x + conv(x) legal.
cap.3: p = (k-1)//2 at s = 1 is shape-preserving, the precondition for the additive skip in a residual block.

cap.1: Look at the far border: the bright square meets the blank ring, so the stencil fires there too. The padding itself looks like an edge.
cap.2: Zero padding is dark. Where a bright region touches the border, an edge detector responds to an edge that is not in the photo.
cap.3: Zero padding creates boundary responses wherever the input is non-zero at the border: a known side effect of padding with zeros.

cap.1: Now hop two spaces at a time. Half the spots are skipped in each direction, so the sheet comes out 4 by 4.
cap.2: stride=2 with a 3x3 kernel and padding 1 halves the map: floor((8 + 2 - 3)/2) + 1 = 4. ResNet downsamples this way.
cap.3: L_out = floor((L_in + 2p - k)/s) + 1. The floor silently drops a last partial window, the usual cause of one-pixel mismatches at a skip.

predict.q: An 8x8 photo, a 3x3 stencil, no padding, hop 1. How wide is the score sheet?
predict.why: The stencil must fit inside the photo: 8 - 3 + 1 = 6 spots per row. Padding 1 would give 8 back.

predict.q: You shuffle every photo's pixels with the same fixed shuffle, then train. Which network gets worse?
predict.why: A dense layer never knew which pixels were neighbours. The CNN's advantage was locality, and the shuffle destroys it.

predict.q: Max-pooling slides a window too. What does it lack that a convolution has?
predict.why: Pooling uses the same window and the same L_out formula, but it just keeps the loudest value. There is nothing to learn.

object.where: Every vision network since AlexNet, and the edge detectors interpretability finds in their early layers.
